<|q|>What is the command for rearranging the bar?<|a|>omarchy bar position bottom
omarchy bar background glassy  # opaque, glassy, none, or cycle
omarchy bar move omarchy.weather --section centerBegin --index 0
omarchy bar move omarchy.bluetooth --section tray  # into the tray's drawer
omarchy bar set omarchy.clock format "HH:mm"
omarchy bar defaults          # back to the shipped layout<|end|>

  "version": 1,
  "bar": {
    "position": "top",

    "layout": {
      "left": [{ "id": "omarchy.menu" }, { "id": "omarchy.workspaces" }],
      "centerBegin": [{ "id": "omarchy.indicators" }],
      "center": [{ "id": "omarchy.clock", "format": "HH:mm" }],
      "centerEnd": [{ "id": "omarchy.weather" }],
      "right": [{ "id": "omarchy.audio" }, { "id": "omarchy.power" }]
    }
  }
}<|end|>

Omarchy command center

Usage:
  omarchy <command> [args...]
  omarchy commands [--all] [--json] [--check]
  omarchy <group> --help
  omarchy <group> <command> --help

Common commands:
  omarchy update              Update Omarchy and system packages
  omarchy theme list          List available themes
  omarchy theme set <name>    Apply a theme
  omarchy font list           List available fonts
  omarchy screenshot          Take a screenshot
  omarchy debug               Print debugging information

Groups:
  agent          AI coding agents, their usage, and subscription accounts
  audio          Audio input and output controls
  bar            Omarchy shell bar layout and settings
  battery        Battery status helpers
  bluetooth      Bluetooth device controls
  branch         Omarchy git branch management
  branding       About and screensaver branding
  brightness     Display and keyboard brightness
  capture        Screenshots and screen recording
  channel        Omarchy release channel management
  clipboard      Clipboard helpers
  cmd            Command and shortcut helpers
  config         System configuration helpers
  debug          Diagnostics and support logs
  ...<|end|>

<|q|>How do I keyboard, Mouse, Trackpad?<|a|>hl.config({
  input = {
    -- Use multiple keyboard layouts and switch between them with Left Alt + Right Alt
    kb_layout = "us,dk",
    kb_options = "omarchy:shift_caps_compose,grp:alts_toggle",

    -- Change speed of keyboard repeat
    repeat_rate = 40,
    repeat_delay = 600,

    -- Increase sensitivity for mouse/trackpad (default: 0)
    sensitivity = 0.35,

    touchpad = {
      -- Use natural (inverse) scrolling
      natural_scroll = true,

      -- Use two-finger clicks for right-click instead of lower-right corner
      clickfinger_behavior = true,

      -- Control the speed of your scrolling
      scroll_factor = 0.3,
    },
  },
})

-- Scroll faster in the terminal
o.window("(Alacritty|kitty|foot)", { scroll_touchpad = 1.5 })<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about welcome to Omarchy<|a|>Omarchy is an omakase Linux distribution based on Arch, the tiling window manager Hyprland, and the desktop construction-kit Quickshell. It ships with everything a modern, savvy computer user needs to be productive immediately. From Neovim (btw) to Chromium, Obsidian to LibreOffice, and Hype to Monologue. Hell, even a retro Winamp-style music player is there!<|end|>
<|q|>Welcome to Omarchy<|a|>Omarchy is an omakase Linux distribution based on Arch, the tiling window manager Hyprland, and the desktop construction-kit Quickshell. It ships with everything a modern, savvy computer user needs to be productive immediately. From Neovim (btw) to Chromium, Obsidian to LibreOffice, and Hype to Monologue. Hell, even a retro Winamp-style music player is there!<|end|>
<|q|>Tell me about getting Started<|a|>Omarchy is installed using an ISO. You can choose between a full-disk install, which takes over the entire drive, or a free-space install, which puts Omarchy in the unallocated space on a drive — that's how you dual boot alongside Windows or another OS (see dual-boot install — note that you'll need to turn off BitLocker in Windows first). Either way, the installation defaults to full encryption, and the full-disk option will wipe the selected drive, so be sure to take a backup before using an existing one!<|end|>
<|q|>Getting Started<|a|>Omarchy is installed using an ISO. You can choose between a full-disk install, which takes over the entire drive, or a free-space install, which puts Omarchy in the unallocated space on a drive — that's how you dual boot alongside Windows or another OS (see dual-boot install — note that you'll need to turn off BitLocker in Windows first). Either way, the installation defaults to full encryption, and the full-disk option will wipe the selected drive, so be sure to take a backup before using an existing one!<|end|>
<|q|>What is use a wired or 2.4ghz keyboard?<|a|>The full-disk encryption won't allow you to enter the password from a Bluetooth keyboard at startup. Just like you can't use a Bluetooth keyboard to enter the BIOS on a PC. You'll need a keyboard that either uses a 2.4ghz dongle or a cable (which is much nicer for latency anyway!). I personally love the Lofree Flow84!<|end|>

<|q|>What is installing for another owner?<|a|>If you're setting up a machine for someone else — a family member, a new employee, a buyer — you shouldn't be answering the personal questions on their behalf. Hit `Ctrl + C` on the very first screen of the installer (the keyboard selection), and Omarchy will offer to prepare the machine for another owner instead. The system installs right away, but all the personal setup — keyboard layout, username, password — is deferred until the machine boots for the first time.<|end|>

<|q|>What is language?<|a|>Omarchy speaks 50 languages — the same set as omarchy.org — and English is the default. To switch, open the Omarchy menu and go to _Setup > Language_, or run `omarchy language <code>` in a terminal (`omarchy language list` shows the codes). The menu, desktop, and Omarchy's own notifications change language immediately, and every application you open afterwards follows too. Apps that were already open switch once you restart them.<|end|>

The menu, desktop, and Omarchy's own notifications change language immediately, and every application you open afterwards follows too. Apps that were already open switch once you restart them.<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about the Top Bar<|a|>The strip along the top of your screen is the Omarchy bar. It's not a bolted-on status bar but part of the Omarchy shell, the single long-running Quickshell process that also draws the menu, the notifications, the OSD popups, and the lock screen. That's why it themes perfectly with everything else and why a panel opens instantly instead of spawning a new app.<|end|>

<|q|>What is dictation?<|a|>On fresh installs, Superwhisper is the default dictation backend, using cloud processing without offline model downloads. Choose Superwhisper or Voxtype through _Setup > Defaults > Dictation_ in the Omarchy menu. Selecting a backend installs it if needed and makes it the default for dictation. Voxtype loads a base English model that takes up 150MB; change the model with `voxtype setup model` and other settings through `~/.config/voxtype/config.toml`. Superwhisper opens its settings to choose cloud or local processing, and OPR keeps the application updated.<|end|>

<|q|>What is starting Neovim?<|a|>You can start Neovim using `Super + Shift + N` (the binding launches your default editor, which is Neovim out of the box), but it's usually easier to drive it from the terminal by navigating to the directory you wish to work in and typing `n`. The `n` is the alias for `nvim`, which will use the the present directory to open by default. You can open a single file with `n myfile.txt`.<|end|>

<|q|>What is installing and updating agents?<|a|>Except for Hermes, these agents use mise's lazy installation: the first launch installs the CLI, and later launches reuse it. mise also checks an installed agent for a new release at most once every four hours, just before it starts or in the background at a shell prompt. If that update fails or you're offline, the installed version runs. `omarchy update` updates installed agents with the rest of Omarchy, and `mup` updates mise-managed tools only.<|end|>

<|q|>What is crash diagnosis?<|a|>Omarchy watches systemd-coredump for process crashes. When something segfaults, you'll get a "Process crashed" notification — click it, and the crash is handed to your default agent along with Omarchy's diagnose-crash skill, which walks the agent through establishing the facts from the core dump and deciding whether the crash is worth reporting upstream. You can also run it by hand against any PID from `coredumpctl list` with `omarchy agent crash <pid>`.<|end|>

<|q|>What is the Omarchy Skill?<|a|>Agent skills help AI use specific tools in a specific way, and Omarchy ships with a default skill for tailoring the system. It's symlinked into the skill directories for Claude Code (`~/.claude/skills`), Codex (`~/.codex/skills`), Pi (`~/.pi/agent/skills`), Antigravity (`~/.gemini/config/skills`), Hermes (`~/.hermes/skills` and each `~/.hermes/profiles/*/skills`), and the generic `~/.agents/skills` location, so most harnesses pick it up automatically.<|end|>

<|q|>What is using your own installation?<|a|>mise's commands come before `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`, so a tool you installed yourself, for example with Claude Code's or Cursor's own installer, still runs mise's copy. Apps launched from the desktop also find mise's commands before system packages, so an app that runs `gh` gets mise's copy even if you installed `github-cli` with pacman, and mise installs that copy the first time. <|q|>What is removing and restoring defaults?<|a|>_Remove Preinstalls_ has mise skip Omarchy's tool declarations for your user, by adding them to `ignored_config_paths` in `~/.config/mise/miserc.toml`. _Restore Preinstalls_ removes that line again. Tools you declare yourself, in your own config or in a project's `mise.toml`, keep working either way. If you choose a default agent or set up Python after removing the preinstalls, that tool is added to your own config. Both apply only to your user; other users on the machine keep their own choice.<|end|>

<|q|>What is four channels?<|a|>Omarchy is updated along four channels: stable, RC, edge, and dev. New installations start on the stable channel, which tracks the official releases, as well as the stable Omarchy Arch mirror that's running one month behind the latest, so we can catch any new incompatibilities that require config changes before they cause problems for people.<|end|>

<|q|>What is firmware updates?<|a|>Your packages aren't the only thing that goes stale. Many laptops and peripherals ship BIOS, SSD, and dock firmware through the Linux Vendor Firmware Service, and _Update > Firmware_ in the Omarchy menu will fetch and install whatever your hardware has waiting. It installs `fwupd` the first time you run it. Plenty of firmware can only be written during a reboot, so don't be surprised to be asked for one.<|end|>

<|q|>What is warning about direct pacman/yay updates?<|a|>If you're already familiar with Arch, you might be tempted to just run `pacman -Syu` or `yay -Syu` yourself, but if you do that, you'll miss the snapshot, migrations, and configuration updates that Omarchy runs together with new packages. That's why Omarchy will actually stop a direct system upgrade and point you to `omarchy update` instead. (If you really know what you're doing, the guard will tell you how to bypass it for a single transaction.)<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about dotfiles<|a|>Omarchy is primarily configured through the so-called dotfiles that live in `~/.config`. Those are considered your files for your changes. The files that live in `/usr/share/omarchy` belong to Omarchy itself, and you shouldn't be messing with those. If you need to change anything in `/usr/share/omarchy`, you should be overwriting the value in `~/.config` instead.<|end|>
<|q|>Dotfiles<|a|>Omarchy is primarily configured through the so-called dotfiles that live in `~/.config`. Those are considered your files for your changes. <|q|>What is changing internal Omarchy files?<|a|>Look, this is your computer. You can do whatever you want with it, but I would advise against making changes to the files in `/usr/share/omarchy` directly. They belong to the Omarchy pacman package, so your changes will simply be overwritten on the next update. You're better off just overwriting any default values you don't like in the `~/.config/*` folder instead.<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about shell Plugins<|a|>The Omarchy desktop runs as a single long-lived Quickshell process called `omarchy-shell`, and almost everything you see on screen is a plugin inside it. The bar is a plugin. So are the panels that drop down from it, the fullscreen overlays like the emoji picker and the clipboard manager, the Omarchy menu itself, the lock screen, the polkit dialog, and the headless services that watch your battery and warm your screen up at night.<|end|>
<|q|>Shell Plugins<|a|>The Omarchy desktop runs as a single long-lived Quickshell process called `omarchy-shell`, and almost everything you see on screen is a plugin inside it. The bar is a plugin. So are the panels that drop down from it, the fullscreen overlays like the emoji picker and the clipboard manager, the Omarchy menu itself, the lock screen, the polkit dialog, and the headless services that watch your battery and warm your screen up at night.<|end|>

<|q|>What is chinese, Japanese, and Korean?<|a|>Chinese, Japanese, and Korean share many characters but draw some of them differently, so the same character looks right to one reader and foreign to another. Picking one of these languages under _Setup > Language_, or its input method, sets the matching forms. To choose them yourself, run `omarchy font cjk jp`, `kr`, `sc`, `tc` (Taiwan), or `hk` (Hong Kong) in a terminal; `omarchy font cjk default` goes back to the system's choice, which is Japanese forms.<|end|>

<|q|>Why are some apps so large on my display?<|a|>Omarchy assumes a 2x high-resolution display, which requires setting `GDK_SCALE` to 2 in `~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua`. But if you're on a 1x display, you can change `local omarchy_gdk_scale = 2` to 1 (and then restart any app that's oversized). See the manual on monitors.<|end|>

<|q|>What is changing your passwords?<|a|>You have two passwords on an encrypted install: the one that unlocks the drive at boot, and the one you log in and `sudo` with. Setup makes them the same. Both can be changed under _Update > Password_ in the Omarchy menu — _Drive Encryption_ for the first, _User_ for the second. Changing the drive password asks for the current one first, so have it handy. If a change is interrupted, run _Drive Encryption_ again: it asks for the password that unlocks the drive now and finishes the change.<|end|>

<|q|>What is passing on a machine you've already used?<|a|>If you're handing your machine over to someone else, you don't have to reinstall it. Run _Setup > Reset Computer_ in the Omarchy menu, type `reset` to confirm, and reboot. That wipes every user account and everything in `/home`, throws away all the packages and system changes you made since installation, and clears the machine's identity — network connections, host keys, and all. What comes back up is the setup wizard from the first boot, ready for its new owner to enter their own name, password, and encryption password.<|end|>

<|q|>What is passwordless sudo?<|a|>Sometimes you want `sudo` to stop asking, most often when an AI agent is doing a long stretch of system work for you. _Setup > Security > Passwordless Sudo_ asks how long to allow access: 15 minutes, 1 Hour, 1 Day, or Permanently. A red warning icon appears beside the other menu bar indicators while access is active. Click it or run the command again to turn access off. You can also pass your own number of minutes (from 1 to 1440) with `omarchy-sudo-passwordless 30`, or use `omarchy-sudo-passwordless permanent`.<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about unattended Installs<|a|>The Omarchy ISO can install itself with nobody at the keyboard. If the installer finds a second drive labeled `cidata` carrying its configuration files, it copies them off, skips the setup wizard entirely, and reboots into the finished system on its own. No special ISO build, no extra boot menu entry — with no such drive attached, nothing changes and you get the normal wizard.<|end|>

<|q|>What is SSH access?<|a|>When `authorized_keys` is present, the install sets the keys up as the user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, enables `sshd`, and opens the firewall for it. (A stock Omarchy install ships openssh with the service disabled and the port closed, so an unattended machine would otherwise be unreachable.) The install only adds your keys — it doesn't loosen any of the SSH daemon's other authentication settings.<|end|>

Omarchy command center

Usage:

  omarchy theme set <name>    Apply a theme
  omarchy font list           List available fonts
  omarchy screenshot          Take a screenshot

  bluetooth      Bluetooth device controls
  branch         Omarchy git branch management

  channel        Omarchy release channel management

  cmd            Command and shortcut helpers
  config         System configuration helpers
  debug          Diagnostics and support logs
  ...<|end|>

<|q|>How do I keyboard, Mouse, Trackpad right now?<|a|>hl.config({
  input = {
    -- Use multiple keyboard layouts and switch between them with Left Alt + Right Alt
    kb_layout = "us,dk",
    kb_options = "omarchy:shift_caps_compose,grp:alts_toggle",

    -- Change speed of keyboard repeat
    repeat_rate = 40,
    repeat_delay = 600,

    -- Increase sensitivity for mouse/trackpad (default: 0)
    sensitivity = 0.35,

    touchpad = {
      -- Use natural (inverse) scrolling
      natural_scroll = true,

      -- Use two-finger clicks for right-click instead of lower-right corner
      clickfinger_behavior = true,

      -- Control the speed of your scrolling
      scroll_factor = 0.3,
    },
  },
})

-- Scroll faster in the terminal
o.window("(Alacritty|kitty|foot)", { scroll_touchpad = 1.5 })<|end|>

<|q|>Tell me about welcome to Omarhcy<|a|>Omarchy is an omakase Linux distribution based on Arch, the tiling window manager Hyprland, and the desktop construction-kit Quickshell. It ships with everything a modern, savvy computer user needs to be productive immediately. From Neovim (btw) to Chromium, Obsidian to LibreOffice, and Hype to Monologue. Hell, even a retro Winamp-style music player is there!<|end|>
<|q|>on omarchy tell me about welcome to Omarchy<|a|>Omarchy is an omakase Linux distribution based on Arch, the tiling window manager Hyprland, and the desktop construction-kit Quickshell. <|q|>Tell me getting about Started<|a|>Omarchy is installed using an ISO. You can choose between a full-disk install, which takes over the entire drive, or a free-space install, which puts Omarchy in the unallocated space on a drive — that's how you dual boot alongside Windows or another OS (see dual-boot install — note that you'll need to turn off BitLocker in Windows first). Either way, the installation defaults to full encryption, and the full-disk option will wipe the selected drive, so be sure to take a backup before using an existing one!<|end|>

<|q|>What is language on this machine?<|a|>Omarchy speaks 50 languages — the same set as omarchy.org — and English is the default. To switch, open the Omarchy menu and go to _Setup > Language_, or run `omarchy language <code>` in a terminal (`omarchy language list` shows the codes). The menu, desktop, and Omarchy's own notifications change language immediately, and every application you open afterwards follows too. Apps that were already open switch once you restart them.<|end|>

<|q|>what is indicators?<|a|>The little cluster in the center is the indicators widget. These are status glyphs for modes you've turned on: do not disturb, night light, a queued reminder, an active screen recording, stay awake, and dictation. It installs the CLI if it's missing. The first account for a provider signs in through your normal browser, right where the CLI always looks.<|end|>

<|q|>What crash diagnosis?<|a|>Omarchy watches systemd-coredump for process crashes. When something segfaults, you'll get a "Process crashed" notification — click it, and the crash is handed to your default agent along with Omarchy's diagnose-crash skill, which walks the agent through establishing the facts from the core dump and deciding whether the crash is worth reporting upstream. You can also run it by hand against any PID from `coredumpctl list` with `omarchy agent crash <pid>`.<|end|>

<|q|>What is local LLMs in omarchy?<|a|>Omarchy recommends two ways of running local LLM models: LM Studio and Ollama. LM Studio provides a GUI interface for finding open-weight models, installing them, and running them. It's a great way to get going easily. Ollama offers a CLI for doing so similarly. But if you're new to local models, I'd start with LM Studio. You can install either under _Install > AI_ in the Omarchy Menu.<|end|>

<|q|>What the is Omarchy Skill?<|a|>Agent skills help AI use specific tools in a specific way, and Omarchy ships with a default skill for tailoring the system. Like tweaking your Hyprland config, adjusting the bar, or even creating a new theme from scratch. It's symlinked into the skill directories for Claude Code (`~/.claude/skills`), Codex (`~/.codex/skills`), Pi (`~/.pi/agent/skills`), Antigravity (`~/.gemini/config/skills`), Hermes (`~/.hermes/skills` and each `~/.hermes/profiles/*/skills`), and the generic `~/.agents/skills` location, so most harnesses pick it up automatically.<|end|>

<|q|>What is aternative Editors?<|a|>Omarchy ships with Neovim by default, but if you'd like something a bit more mainstream and familiar, you can run the Omarchy Menu (`Super + Space`) and see the options under _Install > Editor_. <|q|>is preinstalled CLI tools?<|a|>Omarchy makes tools such as `gh`, `uv`, and most coding agents available through mise's lazy installation. The first time you run one, mise installs it. Later runs reuse the installed version; they do not check for an update on every launch.<|end|>

<|q|>What using is your own installation?<|a|>mise's commands come before `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`, so a tool you installed yourself, for example with Claude Code's or Cursor's own installer, still runs mise's copy. Apps launched from the desktop also find mise's commands before system packages, so an app that runs `gh` gets mise's copy even if you installed `github-cli` with pacman, and mise installs that copy the first time. To use yours instead, disable mise's copy in `~/.config/mise/config.toml`. For example, if you installed Cursor CLI yourself:<|end|>

Tools you declare yourself, in your own config or in a project's `mise.toml`, keep working either way. If you choose a default agent or set up Python after removing the preinstalls, that tool is added to your own config. Both apply only to your user; other users on the machine keep their own choice.<|end|>

<|q|>What is sharing files if possible?<|a|>The directory `~/Windows` in your home directory is automatically shared with the VM. Put files there if you want them accessible to Windows. The VM has no access to any other part of your file system, so you're safe from anything nasty on the Windows side. Its own virtual disk is available at `~/.windows`.<|end|>

They belong to the Omarchy pacman package, so your changes will simply be overwritten on the next update. You're better off just overwriting any default values you don't like in the `~/.config/*` folder instead.<|end|>

<|q|>What chinese, Japanese, and Korean?<|a|>Chinese, Japanese, and Korean share many characters but draw some of them differently, so the same character looks right to one reader and foreign to another. Picking one of these languages under _Setup > Language_, or its input method, sets the matching forms. To choose them yourself, run `omarchy font cjk jp`, `kr`, `sc`, `tc` (Taiwan), or `hk` (Hong Kong) in a terminal; `omarchy font cjk default` goes back to the system's choice, which is Japanese forms.<|end|>

<|q|>why are some apps so large on my display?<|a|>Omarchy assumes a 2x high-resolution display, which requires setting `GDK_SCALE` to 2 in `~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua`. But if you're on a 1x display, you can change `local omarchy_gdk_scale = 2` to 1 (and then restart any app that's oversized). See the manual on monitors.<|end|>

<|q|>can you tell me why can't I login or sudo with my password?<|a|>You probably typed it wrong too many times and got locked out. If this is happening on the lock screen, you can hit `CTRL + ALT + F2` to start a new TTY where you can login as root, then run `faillock --reset --user [your-username]`. That'll reset the lockout, and you're good to go.<|end|>

<|q|>What is changing your passwords right now?<|a|>You have two passwords on an encrypted install: the one that unlocks the drive at boot, and the one you log in and `sudo` with. Setup makes them the same. Both can be changed under _Update > Password_ in the Omarchy menu — _Drive Encryption_ for the first, _User_ for the second. Changing the drive password asks for the current one first, so have it handy. If a change is interrupted, run _Drive Encryption_ again: it asks for the password that unlocks the drive now and finishes the change.<|end|>

<|q|>What is psasing on a machine you've already used?<|a|>If you're handing your machine over to someone else, you don't have to reinstall it. Run _Setup > Reset Computer_ in the Omarchy menu, type `reset` to confirm, and reboot. That wipes every user account and everything in `/home`, throws away all the packages and system changes you made since installation, and clears the machine's identity — network connections, host keys, and all. What comes back up is the setup wizard from the first boot, ready for its new owner to enter their own name, password, and encryption password.<|end|>

<|q|>what is passwordless sudo?<|a|>Sometimes you want `sudo` to stop asking, most often when an AI agent is doing a long stretch of system work for you. _Setup > Security > Passwordless Sudo_ asks how long to allow access: 15 minutes, 1 Hour, 1 Day, or Permanently. A red warning icon appears beside the other menu bar indicators while access is active. Click it or run the command again to turn access off. You can also pass your own number of minutes (from 1 to 1440) with `omarchy-sudo-passwordless 30`, or use `omarchy-sudo-passwordless permanent`.<|end|>
